# Write for the habit, not just the click

James Clear · Customer insight · `clear-habit-laws`

In Atomic Habits, James Clear describes four laws of behavior change, tied to the four stages of a habit (cue, craving, response, reward): make it obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying. Use them when the copy should bring readers back – in onboarding, reminders and newsletters.

**Use when:** When customers sign up but never get started, when a product depends on regular use, or in welcome emails and reminders.

**Keep in mind:** When the reader is making a one-off decision, such as requesting a quote – use Fogg’s model for the next step instead. Don’t promise habits or results the product can’t deliver.

## Principles

- Make it obvious (the cue). Tie the action to a moment the reader already has: “After you send your last invoice of the month, upload your receipts.” A time, a place or an existing habit beats “whenever suits you.”
- Make it attractive (the craving). Show what the reader gets straight away, or pair the new habit with something they already want to do. Speak to who the reader becomes: habits that confirm an identity last longer than habits aimed only at a goal.
- Make it easy (the response). Describe a first version that takes under two minutes (Clear’s two-minute rule) and remove steps in the way. “Snap one receipt” is easier to start than “get your books in order.”
- Make it satisfying (the reward). Confirm straight away when something is done and show progress. What is rewarded immediately is easier to repeat.
- Invert the laws when the reader wants to stop something: make it invisible, unattractive, difficult and unsatisfying – and describe only help the product actually gives.

## Choose a move for the situation

- The customer has signed up but not started: The two-minute version.
- The customer starts but forgets: Stack it on a habit and Time and place.
- The customer does it a few times and stops: A reward straight away and Visible progress.
- The customer has kept going for a long time: Who the reader becomes.

## Moves

- **Stack it on a habit.** Clear calls it habit stacking: the new thing comes after something the reader already does. “When you’ve finished your morning coffee, open the app and do today’s five words.”
- **Time and place.** Ask the reader to decide when and where. An occasion is easier to keep than a resolution. “Pick a time. We’ll remind you at 7:30 a.m. on weekdays.”
- **The two-minute version.** Clear’s two-minute rule: shrink the first step until it takes under two minutes. “Five words a day. It takes two minutes.”
- **A reward straight away.** Say what the reader has just managed, the moment it is done. “Five words done. Now you can order a coffee in Italian.”
- **Visible progress.** Show how far the reader has come and what the next step is. “Day 4 of 7. You’ve learned 20 words.”
- **Who the reader becomes.** Clear holds that habits last longer when they confirm an identity. Describe the person as well as the goal. “Seven days in a row. You’re someone who practices every day.”

## Questions to ask

- At which existing moment should the reader do this?
- What does a two-minute version of the action look like?
- What does the reader get straight away once it’s done?
- Who does the reader become by doing this regularly?

## Fictional example

Fictional: in the Ledger & Co. app, clients photograph receipts, which the firm then enters in the books.

- **Before:** Get started with smart receipt management and take control of your finances!
- **After:** Every Friday when you close your laptop: snap this week’s receipts. It takes two minutes, and we’ll enter them for you.
- **Why:** The copy ties the action to a moment, makes it small and says what the reader gets straight away, instead of promising control.

## A complete example

Fictional: the language app Parla teaches Italian. Facts in the brief: five words a day, a session takes about two minutes, the reminder can be set for any time, the first week covers everyday phrases for cafés and restaurants. The copy is the welcome email after sign-up.

> Subject line: Your first five words
>
> Hi!
>
> Today you’ll learn five words. It takes two minutes.
>
> Do it right after something you already do every morning, like finishing your coffee. Pick a time in the app and we’ll remind you then.
>
> By the end of the week you’ll be able to order at a café in Rome: coffee, water, the check, thank you.
>
> [Do today’s five words]
>
> You’ll hear from us at the same time tomorrow.

**What the example does:**

- The email asks for one action, and it takes two minutes.
- The action is tied to the morning coffee and to a time the reader picks.
- The reward is concrete and close: what the reader can do after a week, not fluent Italian.

## Common mistakes

- Welcome emails that list every feature instead of asking for one small action.
- Reminders with no occasion. “Don’t forget to practice!” doesn’t say when.
- Guilt as the driver. “You’ve missed three days” gives the reader a reason to switch the reminders off.
